reports.subject: Agent harness — trace-ledger gatekeeper
reports.summary: The gatekeeper that decides what may be appended to our agent harness's trace ledger must refuse any entry whose stated origin is blank or unregistered for its lane — and a refusal must leave the ledger untouched. Proved in Lean 4 against the strengthened code, including the fail-closed case: an empty or unreadable registry refuses everything.
reports.method: Lean 4 formal proof (toolchain v4.22.0), checked by the Lean kernel. The proof compiles with no placeholder steps (no sorry, no admit) and depends on no axioms beyond Lean's core three. The subject of the proof is the gatekeeper's append-path decision logic, modelled step for step from the code as built.
reports.context: This law was first proved on 2026-11-14 in a weaker form: an entry needed only a non-blank origin. Comparing the claim against the code showed the weaker form was all the code enforced, so the code was strengthened first — origins must now be registered per lane, fail-closed — and the stronger law was then proved against the strengthened code. Both proofs stand; this report states the current, stronger law.
proven: A blank origin is refused, by name. An entry whose stated origin (its provenance) is empty or all whitespace is turned away, and the refusal carries the reason.

An unregistered origin is refused, by name. An entry whose stated origin is not on the registered list for its lane is turned away with a refusal that names the origin and the lane. Registration for a different lane does not count.
Acceptance means a registered origin. Every entry the gatekeeper accepts carries an origin string that is registered for its lane — and therefore non-blank.
A refusal leaves the ledger untouched. When the gatekeeper refuses, no append happens: the ledger's state after the refusal is exactly what it was before.
An empty or unreadable registry refuses everything. If the registered-origin list is empty — or cannot be loaded at all — every candidate entry is refused. The gate fails closed.
not_proven: Membership is not signing. The proof establishes that an accepted entry's origin string is on the registered list. It does not establish that the named origin actually wrote the entry: there is no signature anywhere in this append path, no key, and no check that would catch a caller simply claiming a registered string.

The proof is about a model of the code, not the running code itself. The model mirrors the gatekeeper's decision logic step for step, and the correspondence is documented and reviewed — but it is not itself machine-checked. A proof of the model is not a proof of the running program.

Writing and storage sit outside the proof. The 'ledger untouched' result covers refusals, where nothing is written. A failure during the write itself — for example a storage error part-way through an append — could leave a partial record; neither the code nor the proof rules that out.
Concurrency sits outside the proof. The gatekeeper takes no lock; two writers appending at the same moment are not covered by these theorems.

The module's own path is what is covered. The ledger is a file, and the proof covers appends that go through the gatekeeper. It cannot prevent other code from writing to the file directly: 'appends only through the gatekeeper' is a property of the module's own paths, not a boundary the proof enforces.

The hash chain is a separate law, not claimed here. That a later edit to a recorded entry is detected by the chain is a different property, and this proof does not cover it. That property has its own published reports in this register: the chain immutability proof, and the anchored chain proof that answers the chain's own stated boundary. The chain is hash-linked; it is not signed.

reports.subject: Agent harness — trace-ledger hash chain
reports.summary: Every entry in our agent harness's trace ledger is hash-linked to the entry before it: each entry's stored hash is computed over its own content and the hash it points back to. Proved in Lean 4: if any entry's content no longer matches its stored hash, or any link in the chain is broken, verification fails at exactly the first failing entry — and a pass means every check holds along the whole chain. The boundary is stated on the report: this proves detection of alteration in a ledger as presented, not protection against a wholesale rewrite.
reports.method: Lean 4 formal proof (toolchain v4.22.0), checked by the Lean kernel. The proof compiles with no placeholder steps (no sorry, no admit) and depends on no axioms beyond Lean's core three; two of its results depend on no axioms at all. The subject of the proof is the chain-verification walk, modelled step for step from the code as built: the six checks each entry faces, their order, and the state threaded from entry to entry. The hash function is modelled abstractly — the proof is about the walk, not about SHA-256.
reports.context: The gatekeeper report in this register names the hash chain as a separate law, not claimed there; this is that law's own report. The claim under examination described the ledger as a 'signed hash chain'. Checked against the code, the chain half is real — hash-linked, with unkeyed SHA-256 — and is proved here exactly as built. The signed half is not true of the code: nothing in the append or verification paths signs anything, and there is no key and no signature field. Signing was ruled a separate, later strengthening; this report does not claim it.
proven: Content tampering is detected at the entry. If an entry's stored hash does not recompute from its content as presented, verification fails at exactly that entry's position, named as a recomputation failure — provided the entries before it pass and its own sequence, identity, and link are in order.

A broken link is detected at the entry. If an entry does not point back at the previous entry's stored hash — or, for the first entry, at the chain's starting value — verification fails at exactly its position, named as a link failure.

A pass means the whole chain holds. Verification passes over a ledger exactly when every entry, at its position, passes every check: sequence, identity, link, hash recomputation, and the ordering counters all hold along the entire walk. The equivalence is proved in both directions.

The first failure is the reported failure. If any entry's check fails, verification fails at or before that entry's position; and any failure verification reports is the first failing position, with every entry before it passing. No failing entry is silently passed over.

The harness's own worked example is a theorem. In the harness's test suite, the second entry of a test ledger is rewritten in a copy of the file, its stored hash untouched, and verification is observed to break at position 2. That exact case — first entry intact, second entry's presented content differing from what its hash was computed over — is proved to fail at exactly position 2 with the recomputation reason.
not_proven: A wholesale rewrite would pass. Every result here concerns a ledger as presented, checked against its own internal chain. A ledger rewritten in full — every entry replaced, every hash and link recomputed consistently — passes this verification completely, and no result here says otherwise, because none can: the chain is unkeyed, so anyone can recompute it, and verification has no reference outside the presented entries. The remedy is a reference held outside the ledger; that is the anchored chain report in this register, a separate mechanism with its own boundary.
Verification cannot prove an entry was true when it was written. It proves a ledger was not altered after its entries were committed. A false entry, honestly committed, chains perfectly.

SHA-256 itself is not proved. The hash function is modelled as an abstract function. The detection results rest on determinism alone — the same function, over the same input, at commit and at verification — except for one step: from 'the content was altered' to 'the recomputation differs'. That step assumes, for the pair of inputs involved, that their hashes do not collide. Collision resistance is a standard, believed property of SHA-256; in this proof it enters only as a named assumption, discharged by nothing here, and the content reading of the first result carries it.

The proof is about a model of the code, not the running code itself. The model mirrors the verification walk and the hash construction step for step, and the correspondence is documented and reviewed — but it is not itself machine-checked. A proof of the model is not a proof of the running program.

How an entry becomes the string the hash covers is not proved. The model takes each entry's canonical form as given. In the running code, one fixed serialization produces that form, identically at commit and at verification — a fact read from the code, and the reason the determinism results are about the real system at all. That two different entries could never serialize to the same string is not proved; a serialization collision would defeat the content check before the hash is consulted.

Entries with missing or mistyped fields are outside the model. The model's entries have every field present and correctly typed, so such entries cannot be represented. In the running code a missing field makes verification fail — the detection reading is not weakened — but no theorem here is about them. The ordering counters are likewise modelled as plain whole numbers: the code's handling of negative or non-numeric counter values, which fails verification, cannot be represented in the model, and one counter check in the code reads a JSON true as the number 1, a case the model does not have.

Loading the ledger is outside the proof. The theorems concern a list of entries already loaded. Reading the file and parsing it are not covered — including the path where a malformed line stops the load and the ledger is set aside on the parse error, without this verification ever running. A ledger changing while it is read is likewise outside.

What is done with the verdict is not covered. How the harness's index uses the verdict — marking a broken ledger quarantined, deciding which entries count as verified, answering trusted-only queries — is separate code, not modelled here. The index also keeps its own separate hash chain over its rows; that chain is not proved by this report. That property has its own published reports in this register: the index quarantine proof, and the fixed-code index quarantine proof.
Concurrency sits outside the proof. Verification runs over a loaded snapshot; entries appended while a verification runs, or two writers racing to append, are not covered by these theorems.

reports.subject: Agent harness — anchored trace-ledger chain
reports.summary: The chain report in this register states its own boundary: a ledger rewritten in full, honestly re-chained, passes chain verification, because the chain has no reference outside itself. The harness's answer is anchoring: from time to time, the chain head — the entry count and the head hash at that moment — is recorded in custody outside the ledger. Proved in Lean 4: a rewritten anchored prefix is detected, a new anchor cannot be taken over a changed prefix, a ledger with no anchor never passes, and the entries beyond the latest anchor are counted and stated exactly.
reports.method: Lean 4 formal proof (toolchain v4.22.0), checked by the Lean kernel. The proof composes the chain proof in this register: its model is imported unmodified, not restated, and the chain walk is not re-proved. It compiles with no placeholder steps (no sorry, no admit) and depends on no axioms beyond Lean's core three; seven of its thirteen stated results depend on no axioms at all. The subject is the anchoring decision logic — taking an anchor, and verifying a ledger against its latest anchor — modelled branch for branch from the code as built.
reports.context: The remedy chosen for the chain's boundary was anchoring, not signing. A signing key kept beside the ledger would be readable by whatever could rewrite the ledger, so signing each entry would buy little inside one trust boundary while adding key custody. Anchor records are therefore plain records — an entry count and a head hash — each written to two custodies outside the ledger itself. Signing is deferred, with a named trigger: if these records are ever used as evidence for third parties, or kept between parties who do not trust each other, the anchors — not the entries — are what would be signed. That would be a code change first and a new proof second; nothing here claims it.
proven: Verified means the whole statement. A result of 'anchored-verified', with its stated tail count, holds exactly when: a latest anchor exists; the anchored prefix — the ledger's first entries up to the anchor's count — verifies; the head at that count equals the recorded head; the full chain verifies; and the tail count is the presented length minus the anchored count. The equivalence is proved, not just the safe direction.

A rewritten anchored prefix is detected. If the head at the latest anchor's count differs from the recorded head — or the prefix no longer verifies, or the ledger is now shorter than its anchor — verification reports a mismatch. It never reports verified.

Anchors cannot launder a rewrite. Taking a new anchor when the previously anchored prefix has changed is refused, and nothing is written: the anchor record is left exactly as it was. In the other direction, the record grows only over an intact prefix — a successful new anchor certifies that the previously anchored prefix still stood at the moment of anchoring.
No anchor, no pass. A ledger with no anchor record returns 'unanchored' — a failure result, never a pass.

The un-anchored tail is counted and stated exactly. A verified result carries the number of entries beyond the latest anchor, no more and no less. When that number is positive, the result names those entries as stale; a freshly taken anchor verifies with a tail of zero. 'Stale' is a stated count on a verified result — not a separate verdict, and staleness alone is not a failure.

A break in the tail is named, not passed. If the anchored prefix matches but the chain breaks beyond it, the result is 'chain broken' — never a pass — carrying the same exact tail count; and the break is proved to lie beyond the anchored count, in the tail, since the prefix was just verified.
not_proven: Detection is proved given an authentic anchor record. Every result here assumes the anchor record the verifier reads — its entry count and head hash — is the record that was actually taken, over the history that was actually committed. That the custody copies sit outside the ledger writer's reach — one an append-only record held apart from the ledger, one a copy delivered to the operator's own mailbox — is an assumption about the world, not a theorem. A writer who could also rewrite the custody copies could rewrite the anchor to match a rewritten ledger, and no theorem here says otherwise, because none can: the anchor is data, not a signature. What is proved is the comparison itself: if the anchor record is out of reach, the anchored prefix cannot be rewritten without detection.

One component hypothesis remains named and unproved. Detection is proved at the comparison the code performs — a presented head that differs from the recorded head is caught. The further step, that altering an entry deep inside the prefix and honestly re-chaining the rest must change the head, rests on two properties of the real hash construction: its outputs are fixed-length, so a changed link value inside a hash input cannot be compensated by the entry content that follows it; and no recomputation along the way collides. The model treats hashes as arbitrary strings, where neither property is available, so the step is stated here as the hypothesis it is. The harness's own planted test observes the concrete behaviour; the theorem covers the comparison that behaviour feeds.

Entries after the latest anchor are protected by the chain law alone until the next anchor. A wholesale rewrite of that tail alone, honestly re-chained, passes chain verification and the anchor comparison alike; it is caught when the next anchor is attempted over it — the rewritten tail has become part of the prefix-to-be, and the anchor is refused — or if it breaks the chain. How large the tail can grow is bounded only conditionally: it depends on the anchor step actually running after appends and succeeding. What holds unconditionally is that the tail's size is always counted and stated exactly.

No signing is claimed. The anchor record is plain data in custody: nothing here establishes who took an anchor, and there is no key and no signature anywhere in the anchoring. Signing the anchors is a deferred strengthening with a named trigger, not part of this proof.

The proof is about a model of the code, not the running code itself. The model mirrors the anchoring decisions branch for branch, and the correspondence is documented and reviewed — but it is not itself machine-checked. A proof of the model is not a proof of the running program.

Custody itself is outside the proof. Writing and reading the custody records, their storage and placement, and the delivery of the second custody copy are operations, not theorems. A damaged or truncated custody record is a load error in the code and never reaches the decisions proved here; the same holds for an unreadable ledger. The second copy's failure handling — the anchor stands on the first custody, with the failed leg named — is code behaviour read and reported, not a theorem.

Which records count as a ledger's anchors is outside the proof. The model takes a ledger's anchor sequence as given and proves facts about its latest record. The code's matching of records to ledgers — including its path handling — is not modelled; a fault there would be a selection failure, not a comparison failure, and is not covered.

The verdicts are proved; their wording is not. The proof is about the states the verifier reports. The explanation text attached to each state — including the two different explanations under the one mismatch state — is presentation, checked by reading, not proved.
Concurrency sits outside the proof. Two anchor-takings racing on one custody record, or an append racing an anchor, are runtime matters; the model decides over a snapshot.

The chain proof's boundaries are inherited. This proof builds on the chain model unchanged, so its limits apply here too: the hash function itself is not proved, each entry's canonical form is taken as given, entries with missing or mistyped fields are outside the model, and loading a ledger is outside both proofs.

reports.subject: Agent harness — trace-ledger index quarantine
reports.summary: When our agent harness builds its federated index over the trace ledgers, every ledger's chain is verified and each entry is marked verified or quarantined; queries can then be restricted to verified rows only. Proved in Lean 4: the verified part of a broken ledger is exactly the part of the chain that verifies, with the split at the first failing entry; a trusted-only query never returns a quarantined row; and marking an entry as superseded never deletes it. The boundary is stated on the report: the status rule reads each entry's own recorded sequence number, and the proof found — and states — the one case where that rule marks an entry verified without the chain walk having checked it.
reports.method: Lean 4 formal proof (toolchain v4.22.0), checked by the Lean kernel. The proof composes the chain proof in this register: its model is imported unmodified, and the chain walk is not re-proved. It compiles with no placeholder steps (no sorry, no admit) and depends on no axioms beyond Lean's core three; six of its thirty stated results depend on no axioms at all. The subject is the index build's decision logic — how each entry's chain status is assigned, how superseded entries are resolved, what a trusted-only query returns, and the index's own hash chain over its rows — modelled step for step from the code as built.
reports.context: The claim under examination ran: 'A ledger with a broken chain is quarantined and cannot re-enter the federated index until repaired.' Checked against the code, the mechanism differs from that sentence in two ways, and this report states the mechanism as it is. A broken ledger's entries do enter the index: the part of the chain that verifies is marked verified, the rest is marked quarantined, and the ledger is named in the build report with its break point. Exclusion happens later, at query time, and only for queries that ask for verified rows only. And there is no standing quarantine list to re-enter from: nothing about quarantine persists between builds — each build re-verifies every ledger and re-derives every status — so a repaired ledger is verified at the next build simply because it now verifies. The proof also found one place where the claim's spirit is breached even in the mechanism's own terms; that case is stated in the not-proven list below, not smoothed over.
proven: The verified part of a broken ledger is exactly the part that verifies. Every entry up to the chain's verified-through point passes every check the walk applies — sequence, identity, link, hash recomputation, and the ordering counters — against the state built from the entries before it, and is marked verified in the index. For any count up to that point, the ledger's first entries of that count both pass chain verification and are marked verified.

The split falls exactly at the first failure. The verified-through point is the ledger's full length when nothing fails, and otherwise the position just before the first failing entry — never earlier, never later. The failing entry itself is marked quarantined whenever its recorded sequence number is its position, which covers every failure in its content, link, or counters, and sequence failures that skip forward.

Whether a row is marked verified is characterized exactly. A row is marked verified exactly when its entry's recorded sequence number is at or below the verified-through point, and quarantined exactly when it is above. This is proved as an equivalence — the code's rule with nothing added and nothing removed — and it is the form in which the quarantine law is true; the boundary case it exposes is stated in the not-proven list.

A trusted-only query returns no quarantined row. Whatever the query's other conditions admit, every row it returns is marked verified. The result is proved for every form of the query's time-window condition, because the verified-only condition is a separate conjunct of the query and does not depend on the others.

Resolution never deletes. Every entry of every cleanly loaded ledger appears as exactly one row in the index. Marking an entry as superseded or tombstoned changes only that row's currency flag and records what superseded it; the row remains in the index, its chain status is untouched, and the ledger itself is never modified by the index. The two marks are independent: an entry can be verified and no longer current at once.

The index's own chain detects alteration. The index hash-chains its rows in the same construction as the ledger chain. Verifying that chain passes exactly when every row's link and recomputation hold; a failure is the first failure, at its position; and a row whose content was altered after the index was written fails recomputation at exactly its position — under the named no-collision assumption described in the not-proven list, as in the chain report.

The harness's own test cases are theorems. The test ledger whose second entry is rewritten: the first entry's row is verified, the rewritten entry's row and the following entry's row are quarantined, and a trusted-only query over that ledger can return only the first entry's row. The test where a tombstone supersedes an entry in a fully verifying ledger: the target's row is present, marked no longer current, naming the tombstone — and still marked verified. And when every ledger in a build verifies, every row any query returns is verified.
not_proven: One case is marked verified without being chain-checked. The status rule compares each entry's own recorded sequence number against the verified-through point; it never looks at the entry's position. The chain walk stops at the first failure, so it never examines the sequence numbers at or beyond the break. An entry there whose recorded sequence number is duplicated or regressed — at or below the verified-through point — is therefore marked verified without ever having been checked, is counted in the build report's trusted-row count, and is served by trusted-only queries. Ledgers written by the harness's own append path cannot produce this: that path assigns each entry a sequence number equal to its position, so beyond the break the number is always above the point. A hand-crafted ledger file can produce it, because loading a ledger validates nothing about its sequence numbers. This gap was found by this proof, and it has since been ruled that the code be fixed first and the law then re-proved: the fix and its re-proof follow as a separate step, and that step's report will be added to this register when it closes. Nothing here pre-claims either. This report stands unchanged by the ruling — it is the accurate record of the law as proved against the code as it then stood.

A broken index chain is detected, not refused. The query path checks the index's own chain before answering and, on a break, prints a warning — and still serves the results. Detection is proved exactly; no path in the code refuses to answer, so there is no refusal for a proof to establish. This behaviour was likewise found by this proof and is covered by the same ruling described above: the fix and its re-proof follow as a separate step, and this report records the behaviour as proved against the code as it then stood.

SHA-256 itself is not proved. As in the chain report, the hash function is modelled as an abstract function, and the results that read 'altered content is detected' — for a ledger entry, and for a row of the index — rest on a named assumption: that the altered and original contents do not hash to the same value. Collision resistance is a standard, believed property of SHA-256; in this proof it enters only as that named assumption, discharged by nothing here.

Quarantine is re-derived on every build; it is not a state. Nothing persists between builds: each build re-verifies every ledger and re-derives every status from the files as they then stand. A ledger that fails to load at all — a file with a malformed line, for example — takes a stronger path than row-level quarantine: it is named in the build report with its load error and contributes no rows at all, not even the entries that were read before the bad line. The marking proved here applies to ledgers that load cleanly and then fail chain verification.

The proof is about a model of the code, not the running code itself. The model mirrors the index build's decisions step for step, and the correspondence is documented and reviewed — but it is not itself machine-checked. A proof of the model is not a proof of the running program.

Reading, writing, and timing sit outside the proof. Loading the ledger files, writing the index file, and anything that changes while a build runs are not covered; neither is concurrency — two builds at once, or a build racing an append. Some details are abstracted rather than modelled: the query's time-window condition is treated as an arbitrary test, which cannot weaken the exclusion result, since that result is proved for every such test; the build's final ordering of rows rearranges them without changing any row; a few row fields that no part of this law reads are omitted from the model; and the record of what supersedes an entry is modelled as naming its target, where the code asks only that a target be present — the one divergence, an empty-string target, cannot arise for real entry identities.

reports.subject: Agent harness — trace-ledger index quarantine, fixed code
reports.summary: When our agent harness builds its federated index over the trace ledgers, every ledger's chain is verified and each entry is marked verified or quarantined. The quarantine report in this register proved that law against the index code as first built — and found the one case where its status rule marked an entry verified without the chain walk having checked it. The code was then fixed: status is now assigned by each entry's position, and a query over a broken index chain is refused outright. This report is the re-proof against the fixed code, in Lean 4: every entry at or after the first chain failure is quarantined, whatever its recorded sequence number claims; the verified rows are exactly the entries the chain walk checked; and a broken index chain makes the query refuse and serve no rows, in every query mode.
reports.method: Lean 4 formal proof (toolchain v4.22.0), checked by the Lean kernel. The proof composes the earlier quarantine proof in this register: its model is imported unmodified, the clauses the fix did not touch are carried over from it, and what the fix changed — the status rule and the query's refusal — is proved new. It compiles with no placeholder steps (no sorry, no admit) and depends on no axioms beyond Lean's core three; eight of its twenty-nine stated results depend on no axioms at all, including the refusal itself, which is pure control flow over the detection verdict. The subject is the fixed index build's decision logic — how each entry's chain status is assigned by position, what the build counts as trusted, and what a query does when the index's own chain is broken — modelled step for step from the fixed code.
reports.context: The quarantine report in this register is this law's first proof. It proved the law in the form the code then had — status read off each entry's recorded sequence number — and stated the case that form exposed: an entry past a chain break whose recorded sequence number was duplicated or regressed could be marked verified without being checked. The ruling that followed was to fix the code first and then re-prove. The index now assigns status by position, and refuses to answer at all when its own chain is broken; this report is that re-proof. For the code as it now stands, it supersedes the earlier report's characterization of the status rule. The earlier report is not edited by this one: it stands as the accurate record of the law as proved against the code as it then stood — and its proof is what found the case this fix closed.
proven: Nothing at or after the break is marked verified — by position, unconditionally. When a ledger's chain fails, every entry at the first failing position and every entry after it is marked quarantined, whatever its recorded sequence number says. The status rule reads the entry's position and the verified depth only; the recorded sequence number is copied into the row as data and never consulted. This is the quarantine law in its originally stated form — the form the first proof could not establish against the code as first built.

The verified rows are exactly the chain-checked prefix. Every entry up to the verified-through point passes every check the walk applies — sequence, identity, link, hash recomputation, and the ordering counters — against the state built from the entries before it, and is marked verified. The split sits exactly at the first failure, never earlier and never later; on a full pass the whole ledger is verified.

The build's trusted-row count is the verified depth. The count is taken over the built rows' marks, and the marks are verified exactly at the positions up to the verified-through point — so the number the build reports as trusted is exactly the number of entries the chain walk checked, no more and no fewer.

A broken index chain makes the query refuse. Before any query is answered, the index's own hash chain is checked; on a break, the query path refuses, by name, and serves no rows at all — in every query mode, because the check comes first and does not inspect the query's filters. Detection itself is as the earlier reports proved it: a break is the first failing row, named at its position.

An intact index chain means the query answers normally. When the index's own chain verifies, the query returns exactly the rows its filters admit — no more, no fewer — and a trusted-only query over the built rows still returns no quarantined row, for every form of the query's other conditions.

Resolution still never deletes. Every entry of every cleanly loaded ledger appears as exactly one row in the index. Marking an entry as superseded or tombstoned changes only that row's currency flag and records what superseded it; the row remains, the ledger itself is never modified by the index, and the two marks stay independent: an entry can be verified and no longer current at once.

The harness's own test cases are theorems, in their fixed-code forms. The case the first proof found — a ledger broken at its second entry, a later entry's recorded sequence number regressed to 1: that entry is now quarantined by its position, the trusted-row count is exactly one, and a trusted-only query over that ledger can return only the first entry's row; the same theorem also evaluates the old rule over the same ledger and gets 'verified', so the difference the fix makes is itself kernel-checked. One index row altered after the build: every query is refused. An untouched index: queries answer normally. And the earlier cases carry over — the rewritten second entry splits its ledger at one verified row; the tombstoned entry stays present, marked no longer current, and still verified; and when every ledger in a build verifies, every row any query returns is verified.
not_proven: This report supersedes the earlier characterization — for the current code only. The quarantine report in this register characterized the status rule as it then stood; that rule no longer exists in the code, so for the code as it now stands that characterization is superseded by this one. Nothing in the earlier report is edited or withdrawn: it remains the accurate record of the law as proved against the code as it then stood.

The query path has a second refusal, and it is not modelled. If the index file cannot be loaded or parsed at all, the query path also refuses — with an error, before any chain check — and serves no rows. That leg exists in the code, but this proof begins at the loaded rows, as the earlier proofs did; loading and parsing are outside the model, so the load-error refusal is a fact read from the code, not a theorem.

SHA-256 itself is not proved. As in the chain report, the hash function is modelled as an abstract function, and the results that read 'altered content is detected' — for a ledger entry, and for a row of the index — rest on a named assumption: that the altered and original contents do not hash to the same value. Collision resistance is a standard, believed property of SHA-256; in this proof it enters only as that named assumption, discharged by nothing here.

A consistently rewritten index is, to this law, an intact one. The refusal fires on a broken chain. An index file rewritten in full — every link and hash recomputed consistently — is not a break to the check, and no result here claims otherwise; that is the same boundary the chain report states for ledgers. What speaks to wholesale rewrites is the anchoring mechanism, a separate report in this register.

The query path's final recheck is proved vacuous. After a trusted-only query answers, the code re-checks the returned rows and would fail the query if any were not verified. That recheck can never fire on the query's own output: the query's verified-only condition already admits only verified rows, so the recheck removes nothing and changes nothing. It is a dead leg in the code — present, and proved to have no effect.

Quarantine is still re-derived on every build; it is not a state. The fix changed how status is assigned, not when: each build re-verifies every ledger and re-derives every status from the files as they then stand, so a repaired ledger is verified at the next build simply because it now verifies. And a ledger that fails to load at all still contributes no rows, exactly as the earlier report stated.

The refusal is proved as a decision, not as text. What is proved is that no rows are served when the index's own chain breaks. The refusal's exact wording and its exit code are the program's surface — read from the code and exercised by the harness's own tests, not theorem content.

The proof is about a model of the code, not the running code itself. The model mirrors the fixed build's decisions and the query path's decisions step for step, and the correspondence is documented and reviewed — but it is not itself machine-checked. A proof of the model is not a proof of the running program. Reading and writing the files, and anything that changes while a build or a query runs — concurrency included — sit outside the proof, as in the earlier reports.

reports.subject: Agent harness — run supervisor fence
reports.summary: Our agent harness runs long work under a supervisor. The supervisor judges each run only from the artifacts the run leaves behind — its completion and failure markers, its heartbeat, its checkpoint — and when a run stalls it may resume it from that checkpoint, up to a declared maximum number of attempts: the fence. Past the fence the run is preserved and reported, never resumed again. Proved in Lean 4: a run is completed exactly when its own marker says so, a resume is launched only on a checkpoint that verifies exactly, and the fence is never crossed.
reports.method: Lean 4 formal proof (toolchain v4.22.0), checked by the Lean kernel. The proof compiles with no placeholder steps (no sorry, no admit) and depends on no axioms beyond Lean's core three; ten of its stated results — including every planted test case below — depend on no axioms at all. The subject of the proof is the supervisor's classification and stall-response decision logic, modelled step for step from the code as built. One honesty note this register keeps: this proof needed no named assumptions at all. Elsewhere in this register a collision assumption is named wherever a hash is compared; here the checkpoint's hash is derived and carried, never compared against anything, so there is nothing for such an assumption to attach to.
reports.context: The claim this report examines ran: the run supervisor never resumes beyond its declared fence. Checked against the code, the sentence is true — and narrower than the discipline the code actually keeps. The fence is one leg of a four-leg response to a stall — fence spent, no resume mechanism, checkpoint declined, exact resume — and it means anything only alongside the classification soundness and the artifact-only judgment that decide when a stall is real. One clause of the claim's original sketch, that once the fence is reached later passes change nothing at all, turned out false of the code; the law is stated and proved in the code's true forms instead, and the first item of the boundary list below carries that correction in full. This is the fourth law of the harness proof round. The supervisor's events are also mirrored into the trace ledger whose gatekeeper, chain, and quarantine laws are the earlier reports in this register; this proof's counts are over the supervisor's own event record, which is written first and unconditionally, and nothing in it turns on the mirror.
proven: Completion is sound, in both directions. Over a supervisor pass on an active run, the run is classified completed exactly when its completion marker is present, parses as an object, and its status says 'complete'. The completion check comes first: when the marker says complete, no other artifact is consulted for the verdict, and nothing else — no failure marker, no heartbeat state — can complete a run whose marker does not say so.

A present-but-invalid completion marker fails the run — never completes it. If the marker file cannot be parsed, or parses to something that is not an object, the run is classified failed at that pass, with exactly the one failure record the code writes for it and no classification record before it. A marker that parses but says anything else — or says nothing — completes nothing and fails nothing by itself; judgment moves on to the failure marker and to stillness.

The two markers are deliberately treated differently, and the proof keeps the difference. An unreadable completion marker fails the run, as the item above states; an unreadable failure marker is simply ignored — it neither fails nor completes the run, and judgment falls through to stillness, exactly as if the marker were absent. A readable failure marker that says 'failed' does fail the run.

A resume is exact. A resume is launched only when the run's checkpoint verifies in the same pass: the checkpoint state file present and parseable, its step recorded as a whole number, and every required component present in the code's sense — a missing key, an empty string, or an empty object counts as missing, while a value of 0, false, or an empty list counts as present. The launched resume carries the checkpoint's own step and the SHA-256 of the state file's bytes, computed at verification time in that same pass.

An incomplete checkpoint is declined, and the run is preserved. When verification declines, the decline names what is missing, the run is marked preserved, and no resume is launched — not at that pass, and not at any later one, even if the checkpoint is afterwards repaired: preserved is a final state, and the code has no path back from it.

The fence holds as a bound, exactly. Across any sequence of supervisor passes, the number of resumes launched for a run equals the growth of its attempt counter — no more, no fewer: the counter is moved in exactly one place, in the branch that launches the resume, by exactly one, and only from below the fence on an active run. The total therefore never exceeds the run's declared maximum, and every launched resume carries an attempt number at or below that maximum.

At a final state, the supervisor is a fixed point. Once a run's status is completed, failed, or preserved, it is no longer acted on: every further pass leaves its registry record exactly as it stands, records no events for it, and appends nothing. The silence the fence promises holds in full — at the final state, which is where the code places it.

The harness's own test cases are theorems. A run with a fresh heartbeat is judged running and its record unchanged; when its completion marker appears, the next pass completes it. A stalled run with a complete checkpoint is resumed exactly once, carrying the checkpoint's own step and hash. A checkpoint missing one named component is declined with that component named, the run preserved, and no resume launched. At a fence of two, repeated passes relaunch exactly twice and end with the run preserved, and a further pass adds nothing at all. A stalled run with no resume mechanism is escalated and preserved, never completed. And a readable failure marker fails its run.
not_proven: The fence law as first sketched is not what is proved — because as sketched, it is false of the code. The sketch said that once the fence is reached, every further pass leaves the run's registry state and event count unchanged. The registry half holds — a pass that judges a run still running saves nothing — but a run whose attempts are spent is still active, and a later pass with a fresh heartbeat still records a classification event for it: the event record grows while no resume is possible. What is proved instead is the law in its true forms: the bound above, preservation at the first stalled pass that finds the fence spent, and total silence — events and registry alike — only once the run reaches a final state. This report does not claim the sketched form.

Judging by artifacts alone has two halves, and only one of them is a theorem. What is proved: the modelled supervisor's every decision is a function of the declared inputs — the run's registered configuration, the two markers, the heartbeat's stillness, the checkpoint — and checkpoint verification reads the state file only through its step, its hash, and its required components. The other half — that the running code never consults process state: it records the launched process's identity at start and never reads it again, and no process inspection appears anywhere in it — is a fact read from the code and checked by search, not a theorem, and this report does not present it as one.

The resume pin is derived, never compared. There is no stored pin anywhere for a resume to match against: the supervisor computes the pin from the checkpoint file inside the pass, and the resume reads that same computed value. The proof is of the derivation's exactness — that the launched step and hash are the file's own step and the hash of its bytes at that moment — not of agreement with any expectation recorded earlier.

One planted case is named, not claimed. The harness's seventh supervisor case exercises the supervisor driving the mirrored trace ledger — the local event record and its mirror landing together. That composition is the subject of the gatekeeper and chain reports in this register, not of this one; this proof's counts are over the local record, and nothing in it turns on the mirror.

A checkpoint file of the wrong shape can end the pass early, and that path is outside the proof. If the state file parses to something that is not an object, verification raises an error instead of declining, and the supervisor pass stops part-way. The model has no such case — in the model a parsed state file is always object-shaped — so the crash path is named here, not modelled, as with the crash paths named in the earlier reports.

A truth value can pass as a step count. In the language the supervisor is written in, the JSON literal true satisfies the whole-number test, so a state file whose step is true would have that value carried as its pinned step. The model's step is a whole number or nothing and cannot represent the case. It is a margin at the data boundary; no clause of the law turns on it.

Stillness is taken as a single number. The supervisor judges a run stalled by how long its heartbeat has been still, and the proof takes that stillness as given. How it is computed — from the heartbeat file's modification time, or from the run's start when no heartbeat exists, each measured against the pass's clock — is not modelled, and neither is the clock itself. The law governs what the supervisor does with the stillness it computes, not the computation.

The artifacts' authorship is not covered. The supervisor classifies the bytes it finds: a completion marker written by something other than the run, a checkpoint file swapped between passes, a heartbeat touched by another process. The proof covers the classification of what is found, not who wrote it; that the artifacts are the run's own is an assumption about the world the supervisor runs in.

The relaunch itself is outside the proof. The law governs the supervisor's bookkeeping — the resume event, the counter, the pin it carries. Whether the launched command actually restarts the run, and whether the restarted run resumes from the pinned step, is the resumed program's contract; it is exercised by the harness's own tests against the real supervisor, not by this model. That a supervisor pass itself always finishes is likewise not claimed: the model's pass is a total function, while the running pass can block on reading its files.

The proof is about a model of the code, not the running code itself. The model mirrors the supervisor's classification and stall-response logic step for step, and the correspondence is documented and reviewed — but it is not itself machine-checked. A proof of the model is not a proof of the running program. Two supervisors running at once over the same registry and event records — concurrency — sit outside the proof, as in the earlier reports.
